This notebook follows the data through one Stan fit: what goes in, what the
sampler does with it, and what comes out. It runs first on simulated students,
then on HSLS:09, and saves the HSLS:09 draws for the notebooks on posterior
summaries and posterior predictive checks.

Stan samples with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), using the No-U-Turn Sampler
(NUTS) variant. It treats the log posterior density as a landscape and moves a
particle across it, so successive draws can land far apart while staying in
regions of high posterior density. Each chain starts at a random point, adapts
its step size and a scaling of the parameters during warmup, and then records
draws.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(framework)
scaffold() # sources functions/bayes.R

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))
okabe_ito <- unname(palette.colors(palette = "Okabe-Ito"))[c(6, 2, 4, 7, 3, 8, 5)]
options(ggplot2.discrete.colour = okabe_ito, ggplot2.discrete.fill = okabe_ito)

clean <- data_read(
  "inputs.final.hsls_clean",
  col_types = readr::cols(student_id = "c", .default = "d")
)
hsls <- analysis_sample(clean)
regression <- bayes_model("regression")

# One seed for the simulated students
set.seed(505)
```

## The Stan program

The model is in `stan/regression.stan`, shared with the Python project. A Stan
program declares its inputs in `data`, its unknowns in `parameters`, the log
density in `model`, and anything computed from each draw in
`generated quantities`.

```{r}
#| label: program

cat(readLines("stan/regression.stan"), sep = "\n")
```

## Data in

Stan takes a named list whose names match the `data` block. `stan_data()`
builds it from a data frame. The cell builds it for 1,000 simulated students
and shows each entry's type and shape, not its values.

```{r}
#| label: data-in

truth <- list(alpha = 50.4, beta = c(0.7, 1.8), sigma = 6.6)
fake <- simulate(1000, truth$alpha, truth$beta, truth$sigma)
fake_data <- stan_data(fake, WEAK)

describe <- function(data) {
  rows <- lapply(names(data), \(key) {
    value <- data[[key]]
    scalar <- is.null(dim(value)) && length(value) == 1
    data.frame(
      Type = if (is.integer(value)) "integer" else "real",
      Shape = if (scalar) "scalar" else paste(dim(value) %||% length(value), collapse = " x "),
      Value = if (scalar) {
        format(value)
      } else if (length(value) <= 2) {
        paste0("[", paste(round(value, 2), collapse = ", "), "]")
      } else {
        "(array)"
      },
      row.names = key
    )
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

describe(fake_data)
```

`X` holds the two predictors, base-year math minus 50 and SES as supplied, one
row per student, and `y` the
follow-up scores. The rest are switches and prior settings, explained in the
comments of the Stan program. Stan checks the list against the `data`
block: a wrong shape, or a value outside a declared bound, such as a negative
`N`, stops the fit before sampling starts.

## Sampling

`bayes_sample()` runs four chains of 1,000 warmup and 1,000 sampling iterations
each, in parallel. The cell also keeps the warmup draws, which are normally
discarded, to show the adaptation.

```{r}
#| label: sampling

start <- Sys.time()
fake_fit <- bayes_sample(regression, fake_data, save_warmup = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("Sampling took %.1f seconds\n", as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), start, units = "secs"))))
cat(sprintf("Output files: %d CSV files, one per chain\n", length(fake_fit$output_files())))
```

## Draws out

Stan writes one CSV file per chain. Each row is one iteration. The first
columns, ending in two underscores, describe the sampler. The rest are the
parameters and generated quantities.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `lp__` | Log posterior density at the draw, up to a constant |
| `accept_stat__` | Average acceptance probability of the trajectory |
| `stepsize__` | Step size of the trajectory, fixed after warmup |
| `treedepth__` | Depth of the trajectory tree; 2 to the depth bounds the number of steps |
| `n_leapfrog__` | Number of steps in the trajectory |
| `divergent__` | 1 when the trajectory diverged, a sign of a region the sampler cannot explore accurately |
| `energy__` | Hamiltonian energy, used by the E-BFMI diagnostic |

```{r}
#| label: draws-out

# cmdstanr returns the sampler columns and the parameters separately. Bound
# side by side, they hold the same columns as the CSV files.
all_draws <- function(fit, inc_warmup = FALSE) {
  sampler <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit$sampler_diagnostics(inc_warmup = inc_warmup))
  parameters <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit$draws(inc_warmup = inc_warmup))
  tibble(
    chain__ = sampler$.chain,
    iter__ = sampler$.iteration,
    draw__ = sampler$.draw,
    lp__ = parameters$lp__,
    !!!as.list(as.data.frame(sampler)[fit$sampler_diagnostics() |> posterior::variables()]),
    !!!as.list(as.data.frame(parameters)[c("alpha", "beta[1]", "beta[2]", "sigma")])
  )
}

fake_draws <- all_draws(fake_fit)
cat(sprintf("%s rows: 4 chains of 1,000 draws\n", format(nrow(fake_draws), big.mark = ",")))
fake_draws |>
  head(5) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: draws-array

# The same draws as an array: iterations by chains by columns. cmdstanr keeps
# the sampler columns in a second array, fake_fit$sampler_diagnostics().
array <- fake_fit$draws()
cat("Array dimensions:", paste(dim(array), collapse = " x "), "\n")
cat("Columns:", paste(posterior::variables(array), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Sampler columns:", paste(posterior::variables(fake_fit$sampler_diagnostics()), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

## Warmup

During warmup, each chain moves from its random start toward the region of high
posterior density and tunes its step size. The left panel shows the SES slope
over all 2,000 iterations of each chain; the dashed line marks the end of
warmup. The right panel shows the step size, which settles during warmup and
stays fixed after it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-warmup
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.8

with_warmup <- all_draws(fake_fit, inc_warmup = TRUE) |>
  mutate(Chain = paste("Chain", chain__))

ses_panel <- ggplot(with_warmup, aes(iter__, `beta[2]`, colour = Chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1000, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = truth$beta[2]) +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = "SES slope", colour = NULL, title = "SES slope, warmup and sampling (solid line: true value)") +
  theme(legend.position = "inside", legend.position.inside = c(0.98, 0.98), legend.justification = c(1, 1))

step_panel <- ggplot(with_warmup, aes(iter__, stepsize__, colour = Chain)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1000, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Iteration", y = "Step size (log scale)", title = "Step size")

arrange_plots(list(ses_panel, step_panel), ncol = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: early-warmup

# Early warmup iterations of each chain, on the way to the posterior
with_warmup |>
  filter(iter__ %in% c(1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300)) |>
  select(chain__, iter__, lp__, alpha, `beta[1]`, `beta[2]`, sigma) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

Stan starts each chain at random values between −2 and 2 on the unconstrained
scale, so the intercept starts near 0, about 50 points from the posterior, and
$\sigma$ starts near 1. The first proposals are often rejected, so a chain can
stay at its starting point for several iterations. The table shows the chains
climbing toward the posterior, with `lp__` rising by orders of magnitude. In
this run, chains 2 and 4 reach the region of the final draws by iteration 50,
and chains 1 and 3 by iteration 100. Reaching that region is not convergence: the diagnostics in
`06-diagnostics` check that the chains, after warmup, agree with one another.
Warmup runs longer than the climb, because tuning the step size and the
parameter scaling takes longer than finding the posterior. None of the warmup
draws are used for inference.

## HSLS:09

The same steps on the 18,623 HSLS:09 students, with the weak priors. The draws
for the parameters go to the private models folder with `save_model()`, which
records the file in the project database. `07-posterior-summary` and
`08-posterior-predictive` read them back with `load_model()`.

```{r}
#| label: hsls-data

hsls_data <- stan_data(hsls, WEAK)
describe(hsls_data)
```

```{r}
#| label: hsls-sampling

start <- Sys.time()
hsls_fit <- bayes_sample(regression, hsls_data)
cat(sprintf("Sampling took %.1f seconds\n", as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), start, units = "secs"))))
```

```{r}
#| label: save

hsls_draws <- draws(hsls_fit)
saved <- save_model(hsls_draws, "hsls_regression_draws")

# What else a reader of the draws needs: the priors and how the predictors
# were centered, so a later notebook can rebuild predictions on the score scale
settings <- list(
  model = "stan/regression.stan",
  n = nrow(hsls),
  predictors = PREDICTORS,
  w1_math_center = 50,
  priors = WEAK,
  chains = 4,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  iter_sampling = 1000
)
save_model(settings, "hsls_regression_settings")
cat(sprintf("Saved %s draws to %s\n", format(nrow(hsls_draws), big.mark = ","), saved))
print(jsonlite::toJSON(settings, pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = NA))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginals
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 3.2

hsls_draws |>
  pivot_longer(c(alpha, `beta[1]`, `beta[2]`, sigma), names_to = "parameter") |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = okabe_ito[1]) +
  facet_wrap(~parameter, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Draws",
    title = sprintf("Marginal posterior draws, HSLS:09 (n = %s, 4,000 draws)", format(nrow(hsls), big.mark = ","))
  )
```

Each histogram shows one parameter's 4,000 draws. Together the draws are a
sample from the joint posterior: every summary in the later notebooks, from a
mean to a predicted score for a new student, is a calculation done once per
draw and then summarized across draws. `06-diagnostics` checks whether the
draws are trustworthy before anything is summarized.
